## What this notebook does

Our main results compare two samples: the paper's period (June 2005 to March 2016) and our
extension (March 2016 to October 2026). This notebook replaces the other robustness checks as
our **sensitivity analysis**. It asks whether REIT rate sensitivity depends on what the Fed is
doing, and whether the same kind of Fed regime gives the same answer in different periods.

We split the full sample into 13 Fed policy episodes, group them into four stances (hiking,
hold, easing, zero rates) and estimate the two main models in each.

**Before running:** run `replicate_gs.R` first. This notebook reads `results/daily_dataset.csv`,
the exact regression dataset that script writes. Nothing is filled or imputed. The licensed data
are not in the GitHub repo, so get `data/4333_DATA.xlsx` from the group.

**Outputs:** the three results tables below are written as sheets (`FedRegime_Episodes`,
`FedRegime_Stances`, `FedRegime_Wald`) into `results/REIT_RateSensitivity_Results.xlsx`, next to the
main tables. The chart is saved as `results/chart4_fed_regimes.png`. No separate CSVs are written.

To run it: open the project in RStudio, open this file and click **Preview** or **Knit**.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(sandwich)
library(ggplot2)
library(openxlsx)

d <- read.csv("results/daily_dataset.csv")
d$date <- as.Date(d$date)
cat("Days:", nrow(d), "from", format(min(d$date)), "to", format(max(d$date)), "\n")

# Results go into the workbook written by replicate_gs.R; re-running replaces the sheet
WB <- "results/REIT_RateSensitivity_Results.xlsx"
stopifnot(file.exists(WB))   # run replicate_gs.R first
put_sheet <- function(name, df) {
  wb <- loadWorkbook(WB)
  if (name %in% names(wb)) removeWorksheet(wb, name)
  addWorksheet(wb, name)
  writeData(wb, name, df, headerStyle = createStyle(textDecoration = "bold", fontColour = "#FFFFFF",
                                                     fgFill = "#2A78D6", wrapText = TRUE, valign = "top"))
  freezePane(wb, name, firstRow = TRUE)
  num <- which(sapply(df, is.double))
  if (length(num)) addStyle(wb, name, createStyle(numFmt = "0.0000"), rows = 2:(nrow(df) + 1),
                            cols = num, gridExpand = TRUE)
  saveWorkbook(wb, WB, overwrite = TRUE)
}
```

## Step 1: define the Fed regimes

Each episode starts on an FOMC decision date and ends the day before the next episode starts.
The rules:

- A **hiking** episode runs from the first hike of a cycle to the last hike, inclusive.
- An **easing** episode runs from the first cut to the last cut, inclusive. Pauses inside a cycle
  stay in that cycle.
- A **hold** runs from the day after the last move of a cycle to the day before the next move.
- A **zero-rate** episode starts on the day the target range first reaches 0 to 0.25%.

The first episode starts at our first data day (the 2004 to 2006 hiking cycle was already
under way). The 2025 and 2026 decisions were checked against the Federal Reserve's statements.
The earlier dates are the standard FOMC decision dates. **Check them against FRED `DFEDTARU`
and `DFEDTAR` before the final slides.**

```{r regimes}
ep <- data.frame(
  episode = c("2005-06 hiking (end of cycle)", "2006-07 hold at 5.25%", "2007-08 easing (GFC)",
              "2008-15 zero rates and QE", "2015-18 gradual hiking", "2019 hold",
              "2019-20 easing (incl. Mar 2020 emergency cut)", "2020-22 COVID zero rates",
              "2022-23 hiking", "2023-24 hold at peak", "2024-25 easing", "2026 hold",
              "Sep 2026 hike"),
  stance  = c("Hiking", "Hold", "Easing", "Zero rates", "Hiking", "Hold", "Easing",
              "Zero rates", "Hiking", "Hold", "Easing", "Hold", "Hiking"),
  start   = as.Date(c("2005-06-02", "2006-06-30", "2007-09-18", "2008-12-16", "2015-12-16",
                      "2018-12-20", "2019-07-31", "2020-03-16", "2022-03-16", "2023-07-27",
                      "2024-09-18", "2025-12-11", "2026-09-16")),
  trigger = c("Data start; last hike 29 Jun 2006", "Day after last hike", "First cut 18 Sep 2007",
              "Range cut to 0-0.25% on 16 Dec 2008", "Liftoff 16 Dec 2015", "Day after last hike (19 Dec 2018)",
              "First cut 31 Jul 2019", "Range cut to 0-0.25% on 15 Mar 2020 (first trading day 16 Mar)",
              "Liftoff 16 Mar 2022", "Day after last hike (26 Jul 2023)", "First cut 18 Sep 2024; last cut 10 Dec 2025",
              "Day after last cut", "Hike to 3.75-4.00% on 16 Sep 2026"))
ep$end <- c(ep$start[-1] - 1, max(d$date))
ep$id  <- sprintf("E%02d", seq_len(nrow(ep)))
stances <- c("Hiking", "Hold", "Easing", "Zero rates")

i <- findInterval(d$date, ep$start)
stopifnot(all(i >= 1))                       # every day falls in an episode
d$episode <- factor(ep$id[i], levels = ep$id)
d$stance  <- factor(ep$stance[i], levels = stances)

ep$days <- as.vector(table(d$episode))
knitr::kable(ep[, c("id", "episode", "stance", "start", "end", "days", "trigger")])
```

The last episode (the September 2026 hike) has very few days. We report it but leave it out of
the tests (rule: an episode needs at least 60 days).

```{r min-n}
MIN_N <- 60
ep$tested <- ep$days >= MIN_N
ep[!ep$tested, c("id", "episode", "days")]
```

## Step 2: the two models

**Model 1 (total rate sensitivity):** REIT return on the change in the 10-year yield.
β × 100 is the % REIT return for a +1pp yield rise.

$$REIT_t = \alpha + \beta \, \Delta Y_t + \varepsilon_t$$

**Model B (bond beta with equity control):** REIT return on the imputed 10-year Treasury return,
the Baa excess return and the S&P 500 return. b₁ is the bond beta (1 = moves like the bond),
b₃ is the equity beta.

$$REIT_t = \alpha + b_1 \, Tsy_t + b_2 \, Exc_t + b_3 \, SPX_t + \varepsilon_t$$

Standard errors are Newey-West with 5 lags (no prewhitening, no small-sample adjustment), as in
`replicate_gs.R`.

```{r models}
hac <- function(m) NeweyWest(m, lag = 5, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = FALSE)
z <- qnorm(0.975)

fit_group <- function(sub) {
  m1 <- lm(reit ~ dy10, sub);             v1 <- hac(m1)
  mb <- lm(reit ~ tsy + exc + spx, sub);  vb <- hac(mb)
  b  <- coef(m1)[["dy10"]]; s  <- sqrt(v1["dy10", "dy10"])
  b1 <- coef(mb)[["tsy"]];  s1 <- sqrt(vb["tsy", "tsy"])
  data.frame(days = nrow(sub),
             total_pct = 100 * b, total_lo = 100 * (b - z * s), total_hi = 100 * (b + z * s),
             r2_yield = summary(m1)$r.squared,
             bond_beta = b1, bond_lo = b1 - z * s1, bond_hi = b1 + z * s1, t_bond = b1 / s1,
             equity_beta = coef(mb)[["spx"]], r2_modelB = summary(mb)$r.squared)
}
```

## Step 3: results by episode

```{r by-episode}
res_ep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(d, d$episode), fit_group))
res_ep <- cbind(ep[, c("id", "episode", "stance")], res_ep)
put_sheet("FedRegime_Episodes", res_ep)

show <- res_ep
num <- sapply(show, is.numeric); show[num] <- lapply(show[num], round, 2)
knitr::kable(show[, c("id", "episode", "stance", "days", "total_pct", "total_lo", "total_hi",
                      "bond_beta", "bond_lo", "bond_hi", "equity_beta", "r2_modelB")])
```

The chart puts episodes of the same stance side by side, in date order, so you can read across
periods within a stance. The dashed line on the left panel is the 10-year bond's own
sensitivity (about −8.6% per +1pp). On the right, a bond beta of 1 means the REIT moved like the
10-year bond, and 0 means no bond-like movement.

```{r chart, fig.width=10, fig.height=6.2, dpi=160}
INK <- "#0b0b0b"; INK2 <- "#52514e"; MUTED <- "#898781"; GRID <- "#e1e0d9"; BLUE <- "#2a78d6"
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(res_ep[, c("id", "episode", "stance", "days")], panel = "Total rate sensitivity (% per +1pp)",
             est = res_ep$total_pct, lo = res_ep$total_lo, hi = res_ep$total_hi),
  data.frame(res_ep[, c("id", "episode", "stance", "days")], panel = "Bond beta b1 (holding S&P 500 fixed)",
             est = res_ep$bond_beta, lo = res_ep$bond_lo, hi = res_ep$bond_hi))
long$panel  <- factor(long$panel, levels = unique(long$panel))
long$stance <- factor(long$stance, levels = stances)
long$label  <- factor(paste0(long$episode, ifelse(long$days < MIN_N, " *", "")),
                      levels = rev(paste0(ep$episode, ifelse(ep$days < MIN_N, " *", ""))))
refs <- data.frame(panel = factor(levels(long$panel)[c(1, 1, 2, 2)], levels = levels(long$panel)),
                   x = c(0, -8.6, 0, 1), lt = c("solid", "dashed", "solid", "dashed"))

g <- ggplot(long, aes(est, label)) +
  geom_vline(data = refs, aes(xintercept = x, linetype = lt), colour = MUTED, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_linetype_identity() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), orientation = "y", width = 0, colour = BLUE, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = BLUE, size = 2.4) +
  facet_grid(stance ~ panel, scales = "free", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "REIT rate sensitivity by Fed policy episode, Jun 2005 to Oct 2026",
       caption = paste0("Dots: estimate. Bars: 95% CI (Newey-West, 5 lags). * Fewer than 60 days, not tested.\n",
                        "Dashed lines: 10Y bond (-8.6% per +1pp, left) and a bond beta of 1 (right).")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = GRID, linewidth = 0.3),
        strip.text = element_text(colour = INK, face = "bold"), strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = INK2), plot.title = element_text(colour = INK, face = "bold"),
        plot.caption = element_text(colour = MUTED, hjust = 0), plot.title.position = "plot")
ggsave("results/chart4_fed_regimes.png", g, width = 10, height = 6.2, dpi = 160)
g
```

## Step 4: results by stance (episodes pooled)

```{r by-stance}
dt <- d[d$episode %in% ep$id[ep$tested], ]
res_st <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(dt, dt$stance), fit_group))
res_st <- cbind(stance = rownames(res_st), res_st)
put_sheet("FedRegime_Stances", res_st)
show <- res_st; num <- sapply(show, is.numeric); show[num] <- lapply(show[num], round, 2)
knitr::kable(show[, c("stance", "days", "total_pct", "total_lo", "total_hi", "bond_beta",
                      "bond_lo", "bond_hi", "equity_beta", "r2_modelB")], row.names = FALSE)
```

## Step 5: are the differences real? (Wald tests)

Each test pools the days in question into one regression in which every coefficient can differ
by group, then tests whether the coefficient of interest is the same in every group.
A small p-value means the sensitivity really differs across those groups.

```{r wald}
wald_equal <- function(dd, group, x, rhs) {
  dd$g <- droplevels(factor(dd[[group]]))
  f <- as.formula(paste("reit ~ 0 + g +", paste0("g:", rhs, collapse = " + ")))
  m <- lm(f, dd); V <- hac(m); b <- coef(m)
  nm <- paste0("g", levels(dd$g), ":", x)
  K <- length(nm)
  R <- matrix(0, K - 1, length(b), dimnames = list(NULL, names(b)))
  for (k in 2:K) { R[k - 1, nm[1]] <- 1; R[k - 1, nm[k]] <- -1 }
  rb <- R %*% b
  W <- as.numeric(t(rb) %*% solve(R %*% V %*% t(R)) %*% rb)
  data.frame(groups = K, chi2 = W, df = K - 1, p = pchisq(W, K - 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}

tests <- list(
  list("Across the 4 stances",          dt,                       "stance"),
  list("Across the 12 tested episodes", dt,                       "episode"),
  list("Hiking episodes, across periods",     dt[dt$stance == "Hiking", ],     "episode"),
  list("Hold episodes, across periods",       dt[dt$stance == "Hold", ],       "episode"),
  list("Easing episodes, across periods",     dt[dt$stance == "Easing", ],     "episode"),
  list("Zero-rate episodes, across periods",  dt[dt$stance == "Zero rates", ], "episode"))

wt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tests, function(t) {
  a <- wald_equal(t[[2]], t[[3]], "dy10", "dy10")
  b <- wald_equal(t[[2]], t[[3]], "tsy", c("tsy", "exc", "spx"))
  data.frame(test = t[[1]], groups = a$groups,
             p_total_sensitivity = a$p, p_bond_beta = b$p)
}))
put_sheet("FedRegime_Wald", wt)
show <- wt; show$p_total_sensitivity <- signif(show$p_total_sensitivity, 2); show$p_bond_beta <- signif(show$p_bond_beta, 2)
knitr::kable(show, row.names = FALSE)
```

## What the results say (run of 23 Oct 2026)

These numbers come from the tables above. If the data change, re-read them from the tables.

1. **The Fed's stance matters for the total sensitivity.** When the Fed is hiking or holding,
   REITs fall when yields rise (−3.5% and −4.8% per +1pp). When it is easing or at zero, they rise
   with yields (+12.8% and +7.4%). The four stances differ strongly (p < 0.001). One reading: in
   easing and zero-rate periods, yields fall on bad growth news, which also hurts REITs.
2. **The same stance gives different answers in different periods.** Easing in 2007-08 gave
   +20.9% per +1pp; easing in 2024-25 gave −4.8%. Hold episodes range from +3.6% (2006-07) to
   −8.3% (2026). The Wald tests reject equality within the hold and easing stances. The stance
   alone does not pin down the sensitivity; the period does too.
3. **Hiking cycles are the exception.** All three tested hiking cycles give a total sensitivity of
   about −2.5% to −4.2%, and the test does not reject equality (p = 0.70).
4. **In the 2023-24 and 2026 holds, REITs moved like the 10-year bond.** They fell 8.1% and 8.3%
   per +1pp, against the bond's 8.1% and 8.0% in the same periods, with bond betas near 1. The
   2024-25 easing in between was less bond-like (−4.8%). In the 2026 hold the S&P 500 also fell
   about 8% per +1pp, so that result is not specific to REITs.
5. **The bond beta (holding the S&P 500 fixed) varies by period, not by stance.** Pooled by
   stance it does not differ significantly (p = 0.10), but it differs across episodes
   (p < 0.001). It was low in 2005-07, during COVID and in the 2022-23 hikes, and near 1 in most
   other post-2015 episodes.

## Notes and limitations

- **Regime dates are a modelling choice.** Moving a boundary by a few weeks changes which days
  fall in each episode. The 2019-20 easing episode includes the COVID crash weeks of
  late February and early March 2020, so it is not a clean "insurance cut" period.
- **Episodes are short.** Several have fewer than 300 days, so their confidence intervals are wide.
  The September 2026 hike is reported but not tested.
- **Newey-West across gaps.** When episodes are pooled by stance, the lag window can reach across
  the gap between two episodes. With 5 lags this affects only a handful of days per boundary.
- **No causality.** A regime is a label for a period, not a shock. Rates, growth and inflation
  move together, so the coefficients describe co-movement.
- **Nothing is filled or imputed.** Every day in the regressions is a day on which all series were
  observed (see the README and Data_Audit sheets of `results/REIT_RateSensitivity_Results.xlsx`).
